summary: Defines an architecture and protocols for privacy-preserving X.509 certificates using a pseudonym, while still letting an authority trace a certificate back to the person who requested it. It is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: You wear a nickname badge at a party, but the host secretly keeps a list that matches nicknames to real names, in case of trouble.

questions: how does a traceable anonymous certificate work
subtitle: X.509 certificates with pseudonyms that can be traced to the real user if needed.

tldr.problem: Users want anonymous X.509 certificates to protect privacy when using PKI-enabled applications, but certificate authorities need the ability to map an anonymous certificate back to its real user if the anonymity is abused.
tldr.mechanism: A pair of authorities (Blind Issuer and Anonymity Issuer) use split-key cryptography and blind signatures to issue certificates. The Blind Issuer knows the user's real identity but not the certificate; the Anonymity Issuer knows the certificate but not the identity. Only by cooperating can they map a certificate to a user.
tldr.outcome: The architecture enables practical privacy-preserving certificates that remain traceable. Neither authority can unilaterally reveal a user's identity, but together they can if the user abuses the anonymity.

facts.label: Key requirement
facts.value: Both authorities must cooperate to trace a certificate

facts.label: Signature scheme
facts.value: Threshold signature with split private key

today: RFC 5636 is Experimental and has not been obsoleted or replaced. The architecture provides a practical way to balance privacy and accountability in X.509 certificates, although widespread adoption is limited.

sections.title: Privacy and Accountability in PKI
sections.content:
Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) is powerful for authentication but creates privacy concerns. Normally a certificate contains the user's real name, which is exposed whenever the user presents it. Even with pseudonyms, a single Certificate Authority knows the mapping between the pseudonym and the real user, making it a potential big brother. RFC 5636 solves this by separating the authorities.

The core innovation is that no single entity has the complete picture: one authority verifies the real identity, the other validates the certificate request. Only by cooperating can they reveal who issued a certificate, and only if there is evidence of abuse.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one authority keeping your real name with your nickname, two separate authorities each keep half the secret. Neither can reveal who you are alone.

sections.title: The Split-Authority Model
sections.content:
A Traceable Anonymous Certificate (TAC) is issued jointly by two entities: a Blind Issuer (BI) and an Anonymity Issuer (AI). The BI acts as a Registration Authority and verifies the user's real identity, generating a unique UserKey (a random identifier that does not reveal the user's name). The AI acts as a Certificate Authority and creates the actual certificate containing a user-selected pseudonym.

The two authorities appear as a single CA to the outside world, sharing one public key via a threshold signature scheme where both must sign to complete a certificate signature. This technical separation makes it difficult for either authority to act unilaterally.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people sit at separate desks. One checks that you are who you say you are; the other signs off on the certificate you asked for. Neither sees what the other knows.

sections.title: The Certificate Issuance Process
sections.content:
The issuance process uses six steps and cryptographic structures called Tokens and blind signatures. A Token is a digitally signed message from the BI that proves the user was authenticated; it includes a UserKey and a timeout.

When a user requests a certificate with a pseudonym, the AI blinds (encrypts) a hash of the certificate, sends it to the BI along with the Token, and the BI signs the blinded hash using its share of the split private key. The BI returns the signed hash to the AI, which then unblinds it and applies its own key share to complete the signature. This technique ensures the BI never sees the certificate contents, and the AI never learns the user's real identity.

The request can use standard formats like PKCS10 or CMC, making the architecture compatible with existing PKI software and protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: You give one authority a secret message sealed in a special way so they can sign it without reading it. They pass it to the other, who unseals it and adds their signature. Now the certificate is complete and nobody had the full picture.

sections.title: Mapping a Certificate Back to the User
sections.content:
If a user abuses their anonymous certificate, the system can be traced in a four-step process. An aggrieved party reports the abuse to the AI, which verifies the evidence and searches its database for the Token linked to the certificate. The AI then releases this Token to the aggrieved party via a secure channel.

The aggrieved party presents the Token to the BI, which verifies its own signature on the Token and searches its database using the UserKey embedded in the Token to retrieve the user's real identity.

This process requires both authorities to cooperate and both to verify that tracing is warranted, adding procedural security on top of the technical separation.
sections.plainLanguage: If you misbehave, the authority who signed you off gives a hint to a referee, who passes it to the authority who verified your identity. Only they can tell who you are.

sections.title: Design Requirements
sections.content:
The architecture meets three key requirements. First, the TAC is a syntactically valid X.509 certificate with a pseudonym in the Subject field, ensuring compatibility with existing X.509 validators. Second, the system prevents users from later denying they requested the certificate, because they must prove control of the private key during issuance. Third, the user's real identity can be determined only with the agreement of both the AI and BI, balancing privacy against accountability.

The document recommends that the BI and AI be operated by different organizations in geographically separate locations with different staff, providing organizational separation to back up the technical controls.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate looks normal, you cannot deny you asked for it, and finding you requires both authorities to say yes.
